# @lab.Title

<!-- AUTHOR: Generated by skillable/build-lab-steps.ps1 from skillable/lab-steps-template.md and the challenges' README.md files: don't edit it, edit those and run the script again. Import this file in Skillable Studio (Edit Instructions > Import from file(s)), or paste it into Code mode. It uses the cloud portal user User1 and the resource group ResourceGroup1: change those names if the lab profile uses others. -->

Find and fix what's broken in an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Automatic cluster, one challenge at a time. In this capture-the-flag lab, each challenge is a realistic fault, already in place in its own namespace of your cluster. You investigate with the tools on your lab VM, restore the expected behavior, and check your work with one command. Every challenge that passes its check is a captured flag.

**Level:** 200, intermediate  
**Duration:** about 3 hours, in rounds of 15 to 30 minutes

## How the lab works

1. A proctor introduces a challenge, what success looks like, and the tools that can help.
1. You investigate on your own, with the evidence in your environment, and restore the expected outcome. Each challenge page has hints that you can expand, and proctors can give more.
1. You check your work with one command. A challenge that passes is a captured flag.
1. At the end of the round, a proctor shows one way to fix the challenge, and explains the troubleshooting path.
1. The room moves on to the next challenge. Challenges are independent, so you can start the next one even if you didn't finish the last one.

## Your lab environment

Everything in the following table is ready for you. You don't need your own Azure subscription or local tools.

| Component | What's ready for you |
|:--|:--|
| Lab VM | Visual Studio Code with GitHub Copilot and the AKS-MCP server, AKS desktop, the Azure CLI, `kubectl`, `kubelogin`, Helm, `ingress2gateway`, the GitHub CLI, PowerShell 7, Git Bash, and WSL with Ubuntu |
| AKS Automatic cluster | **aks-kubecon-ctf**, in resource group **@lab.CloudResourceGroup(ResourceGroup1).Name**, with node autoprovisioning, deployment safeguards, Azure RBAC, workload identity, the application routing add-on with Gateway API, and Managed Prometheus |
| Challenges | Each in its own namespace of your cluster, each with its fault already in place |
| **C:\LabFiles\kubecon26-pre-day-lab** | The lab repository: each challenge's instructions and manifests, and the scripts that check your work and start a challenge over |

## The challenges

<!-- @challenge-table -->

Your proctor tells you which challenge each round uses. C1 to C4 are the core challenges, and A1 to A6 are alternates. Finished a round early? Try an alternate.

## How to use these instructions

- Commands appear as type text. Select the terminal in the lab VM first, and then select a command in these instructions to type it there. Press **Enter** to run it.
- Code blocks show commands to copy or adapt. They're written for bash, and most `kubectl` commands work unchanged in PowerShell. **Tools and tips** describes how to run the bash-only ones.
- Select the checkbox next to each step when you finish it.

> [!Note] You need basic familiarity with containers and Kubernetes: pods, deployments, services, and `kubectl`. Each challenge page describes what's running, what success looks like, and how to check your work.

# Get started

**Estimated time:** 10 minutes

Confirm that you can reach your environment. If any step on this page fails, ask a proctor right away. They can move you to a spare environment.

## Task 1: Sign in to the lab VM, the Azure portal, Microsoft Edge, and other lab VM resources

All of your lab's passwords and IDs are on the **Resources** tab, above these instructions.

1. [] Sign in to the lab VM. On the Windows sign-in screen, select the password box. Then select +++Passw0rd!+++ to type the password, and press **Enter**. If the VM already shows the Windows desktop, you're signed in: go to the next step.

1. [] **Microsoft Edge** opens the Azure portal when the lab VM starts. If it isn't open, open Edge, and go to +++https://portal.azure.com+++. Sign in with the following credentials:

    - **Username:** +++@lab.CloudPortalCredential(User1).Username+++
    - **Temporary Access Pass:** +++@lab.CloudPortalCredential(User1).AccessToken+++

    Leave this tab open. Some challenges use the Azure portal.

1. [] While you sign in, Windows and Edge offer to keep you signed in. Accept each offer, so that you're asked to sign in less often in the rest of the lab:

    - When you're asked **Stay signed in?**, select **Yes**.
    - When you're asked to sign in to Microsoft Edge, select **Sign in**, and enter your Temporary Access Pass again if you're asked to. When you see **Account added to this device**, select **Done**.
    - When you're asked whether to sign in automatically to all desktop apps and websites on this device, select **Yes, all apps**.

## Task 2: Open the lab folder and a terminal

1. [] **Visual Studio Code** opens the lab repository, **kubecon26-pre-day-lab**, when the lab VM starts. If it isn't open, open Visual Studio Code from the taskbar or the Start menu, select **File** > **Open Folder**, enter +++C:\LabFiles\kubecon26-pre-day-lab+++, and open the folder.

1. [] Select **Terminal** > **New Terminal**. The terminal runs PowerShell 7. Unless a step says otherwise, run every command in this lab from this terminal.

## Task 3: Sign in to the Azure CLI and GitHub Copilot

1. [] Check whether the Azure CLI is already signed in:

    +++az account show+++

    If the output shows your lab account, **@lab.CloudPortalCredential(User1).Username**, under `user`, you're signed in: skip the next step. If it says `Please run 'az login' to setup account`, or shows another account, go on to the next step.

1. [] If you're not signed in, run the following command:

    +++az login+++

    A browser tab opens. Select your lab account, **@lab.CloudPortalCredential(User1).Username**, which you already signed in with in Task 1. If you're asked to sign in again, use the same Temporary Access Pass, +++@lab.CloudPortalCredential(User1).AccessToken+++. When the tab says that you're signed in, return to Visual Studio Code.

    > [!Note] `kubectl`, the lab repository's scripts, and the AKS-MCP server all use this sign-in. AKS Automatic clusters use Microsoft Entra ID for authentication and Azure RBAC for authorization, so you reach your cluster as your own lab account.

1. [] Set up single sign-on to GitHub for this lab. In Microsoft Edge, open a new tab (**Ctrl+T**), and go to +++https://github.com/enterprises/skillable-events/sso+++.

    The page says **Single sign-on to Skillable Events**: *Authenticate your account by logging into Skillable Events's single sign-on provider.* Select **Continue**. Edge then shows the Skillable Events enterprise on GitHub, `github.com/enterprises/skillable-events`. If you're asked to sign in with your lab account, use the same username and Temporary Access Pass as in Task 1.

1. [] In Visual Studio Code, select the blue **Sign In** button at the top right, and then select **Continue with GitHub**. Edge opens GitHub. On each page that it shows:

    - **Authorize Visual Studio Code**, which says *From the options below, choose which account you would like to use to authorize this app*: select the green **Continue** button.
    - The next **Authorize Visual Studio Code** page: scroll down if you need to, and select the green **Authorize Visual Studio Code** button at the bottom.
    - **This site is trying to open Visual Studio Code**: select **Open**.

    Visual Studio Code opens, and the **Sign In** button is gone: you're signed in to GitHub Copilot, and you have access to its models.

1. [] Open the Chat view (**Ctrl+Alt+I**) if it isn't open, and select **Auto** at the bottom of the chat window to see the list of models that you can choose from. **Auto** chooses a model for you, so you can keep it.

## Task 4: Connect to your cluster

1. [] Run the following command to list the cluster's nodes:

    +++kubectl get nodes+++

    Every node should show the status **Ready**.

    > [+Help] Expand this section if kubectl asks you to sign in or returns an authorization error.
    >
    > Run +++az login+++ again, and select your lab account, not another account. Then run the previous command again. If kubectl still can't reach the cluster, run the following commands in order, and then run the previous command again:
    >
    > +++az aks get-credentials --resource-group @lab.CloudResourceGroup(ResourceGroup1).Name --name aks-kubecon-ctf --overwrite-existing+++
    >
    > +++kubelogin convert-kubeconfig -l azurecli+++

1. [] Run the following command to list the challenges' namespaces:

    +++kubectl get namespaces -l kubecon.lab/challenge+++

    You should see one namespace for each challenge.

1. [] Optional: see what a check looks like. Every challenge starts **NOT PASSED**, because its fault is in place:

    +++C:\LabFiles\kubecon26-pre-day-lab\scoring\verify.ps1 -Challenges c1 -Quick -NoReport+++

## Task 5: Set up GitHub Copilot

GitHub Copilot is optional, but some challenges suggest an AI assistant. You signed in to it in Task 3. You stay signed in only in this lab VM, which is deleted when the lab ends.

1. [] In Visual Studio Code, open the Chat view (**Ctrl+Alt+I**). If the blue **Sign In** button is still at the top right, sign in as in Task 3.

1. [] In the Chat view, select **Agent** mode, and then select the **Configure Tools** icon. The **aks-mcp** server is listed: it gives Copilot tools for your cluster. The first time it starts, VS Code asks you to trust it: select **Trust**.

    > [!Note] If **aks-mcp** isn't listed, or Copilot can't use its tools, ask a proctor. You can complete every challenge without Copilot.

## Task 6: Join the event leaderboard

Optional. If your event has a leaderboard, your proctors show it on the screen. Join it to have your checks recorded there: it shows your first name and last initial, and the flags that you capture. Skip this task to keep your results to yourself: your checks work the same.

1. [] Run the following command:

    +++C:\LabFiles\kubecon26-pre-day-lab\scoring\join-leaderboard.ps1 -PlayerId "@lab.User.Id" -FirstName "@lab.User.FirstName" -LastName "@lab.User.LastName"+++

    It shows **Joined the leaderboard as**, and the name that the leaderboard shows. You appear on the leaderboard with your first check. If it says that no leaderboard is open, or that its link isn't set up yet, your event doesn't have one right now: carry on, and ask a proctor if you expected one.

# Tools and tips

Come back to this page whenever you need it during the challenges.

## Tools on your lab VM

| Tool | How to use it |
|:--|:--|
| `kubectl` | In the VS Code terminal. Your kubeconfig has one context, **aks-kubecon-ctf**. |
| Azure portal | Your cluster's **Kubernetes resources** pages, **Monitoring** > **Dashboards with Grafana**, and **Insights** |
| GitHub Copilot with AKS-MCP | In the VS Code Chat view, in **Agent** mode, ask about your cluster, for example, *Which pods in namespace c1-store aren't ready, and why?* AKS-MCP runs as you, with your Azure CLI sign-in. AI drafts, you verify: review what it proposes before you apply it. |
| AKS desktop | Start menu > **AKS desktop**: your cluster's workloads, logs, and events in a desktop app |
| `ingress2gateway` | Translates Ingress resources into Gateway API resources |
| Git Bash | Some commands in the challenges use bash syntax, such as `VAR=$(...)` or `grep`. To run them, select the dropdown next to **+** in VS Code's terminal panel, and select **Git Bash**. `kubectl` and `az` work there too. |
| WSL with Ubuntu | A Linux shell with the Azure CLI, `kubectl`, `kubelogin`, and Helm. It has its own Azure CLI sign-in and kubeconfig, so prefer the VS Code terminal or Git Bash for the challenges. |
| Inspektor Gadget | The `kubectl gadget` plugin is installed. Tracing needs Inspektor Gadget in the cluster too: ask your proctor whether this lab has it. |

# Check your work, or start over

## Check your work

Each challenge page ends its success criteria with a check command, which runs the lab repository's scoring script, such as:

+++C:\LabFiles\kubecon26-pre-day-lab\scoring\verify.ps1 -Challenges c1+++

The check runs the challenge's success criteria against your cluster, and shows **PASS** or **FAIL** for each one, then **PASSED** or **NOT PASSED** for the challenge. **PASSED** is a captured flag. A check takes a minute or two, because some checks watch the application for 60 seconds. C3 can wait several minutes for a new node.

- For a quicker, less strict look while you work, add `-Quick`.
- To check several challenges, separate them with commas, such as `c1,a2`. With no challenge, it checks every challenge in your cluster.

> [!Note] If you joined your event's leaderboard in **Get started**, Task 6, each check records your result there, with your first name and last initial. To keep a run off the leaderboard, add `-NoReport`. Runs with `-Quick` are never recorded. To leave the leaderboard, run +++C:\LabFiles\kubecon26-pre-day-lab\scoring\join-leaderboard.ps1 -Remove+++.

## Start a challenge over

To start a challenge over, run its reset command, which runs the lab repository's deployment script for that challenge only, such as:

+++C:\LabFiles\kubecon26-pre-day-lab\begin-challenge\azure-cli-powershell\deploy.ps1 -ResourceGroup @lab.CloudResourceGroup(ResourceGroup1).Name -ClusterName aks-kubecon-ctf -Challenges c1+++

The reset deletes the challenge's namespace, and deploys the challenge again with its fault. Your changes to that challenge are lost, and other challenges aren't touched. A reset takes 2 to 5 minutes. Some resets also reset Azure resources:

| Challenge | The reset also |
|:--|:--|
| C2 | Deletes your gateway and its public IP address |
| C3 | Deletes the challenge's node pool and its nodes |
| A4 | Resets the federated identity credential in Azure |
| A6 | Re-creates the disk and its data |

> [!Alert] Reset only the challenge that you're working on: it doesn't ask you to confirm, and it can't be undone. Use your lab's own resource group and cluster, as in the command above.

# Wrap-up

## What you practiced

- Following the evidence, from what users see to its cause: events, logs from the previous container instance, conditions, and status
- Telling a healthy pod from a working application
- The AKS Automatic platform: node autoprovisioning, deployment safeguards, Azure RBAC, workload identity, the application routing add-on with Gateway API, and Managed Prometheus
- Fixing the cause in the authoritative configuration, without weakening security or isolation
- Using AI assistance with AKS-MCP, and verifying what it proposes

## Learn more

- [Introduction to AKS Automatic](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/intro-aks-automatic)
- [Deployment safeguards](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/deployment-safeguards)
- [Node autoprovisioning](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/node-auto-provisioning)
- [The application routing add-on](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/app-routing) and [Gateway API](https://gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io/)
- [Workload identity on AKS](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/workload-identity-overview)
- [Monitor AKS](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/monitor-aks)
- [Troubleshoot AKS](https://learn.microsoft.com/troubleshoot/azure/azure-kubernetes/welcome-azure-kubernetes)
- [AKS-MCP](https://github.com/Azure/aks-mcp)
